paragraphs: But Balaam’s ass had suddenly found its voice. The topic was an odd one. Grigory had gone out that morning to do some shopping. The shopkeeper Lukyanov had told him about a Russian soldier whose story was in that day’s newspaper. The soldier had been captured somewhere in a remote corner of Asia. His captors threatened him with a sudden, agonizing death unless he gave up Christianity and became a Muslim. He would not deny his faith. They tortured him and flayed him alive, and he died praising and glorifying Christ. Grigory had told this story at the table. Fyodor Pavlovitch always enjoyed laughing and chatting over dessert after dinner, even if it was only with Grigory. This afternoon he was in an especially cheerful, talkative mood. He sipped his brandy and listened to the story, and then he remarked that a soldier like that ought to be made a saint, and his skin sent to some monastery. “The people would flock to see it, and the money would roll in.”

Grigory frowned. He could see that Fyodor Pavlovitch was not moved at all, and was beginning, as usual, to sneer. At that moment Smerdyakov, who was standing by the door, smiled. Smerdyakov often waited at table toward the end of dinner. Since Ivan had arrived in our town, he had done it every day.
“What are you grinning at?” asked Fyodor Pavlovitch. He had caught the smile instantly and knew it was aimed at Grigory.

“Well, my opinion is,” Smerdyakov began suddenly, in a loud voice nobody was expecting, “that if that praiseworthy soldier’s feat was so very great, then in my view there would have been no sin in it if, in such an emergency, he had renounced, so to speak, the name of Christ and his own christening. By that means he would have saved his life, and could use it for good deeds, and over the years make up for his cowardice.”
“How can that not be a sin? You’re talking rubbish. You’ll go straight to hell for that, and be roasted like a leg of mutton,” Fyodor Pavlovitch put in.
At this point Alyosha came in, and Fyodor Pavlovitch, as we have seen, was thrilled to see him.
“We’re on your subject, your subject!” he chuckled gleefully, and sat Alyosha down to listen.
“As for mutton, that’s not how it is. There will be nothing like that waiting for him for this, and there shouldn’t be, if things are done according to justice,” Smerdyakov insisted stoutly.
“What do you mean, ‘according to justice’?” Fyodor Pavlovitch cried, even merrier, and he jabbed Alyosha with his knee.
“He’s a scoundrel, that’s what he is!” Grigory burst out. He glared at Smerdyakov.

“As for being a scoundrel, just wait a little, Grigory Vassilyevitch,” Smerdyakov answered, perfectly composed. “Kindly think about it yourself. Say I am taken prisoner by the enemies of the Christian race, and they demand that I curse the name of God and give up my holy christening. I am fully entitled to decide by my own reason, because there would be no sin in it.”
“But you’ve said all that already. Don’t waste words. Prove it,” cried Fyodor Pavlovitch.
“Soup-maker!” Grigory muttered scornfully.

“As for being a soup-maker, wait a bit with that as well, Grigory Vassilyevitch, and think it over for yourself, instead of abusing me. For the moment I say to those enemies, ‘No, I am not a Christian, and I curse my true God,’ then at once, by God’s high judgment, I become, immediately and specially, anathema accursed. I am cut off from the Holy Church exactly as if I were a heathen. So at that very instant, not only when I say it aloud but when I merely think of saying it, before even a quarter of a second has gone by, I am cut off. Is that so or not, Grigory Vassilyevitch?”
He spoke to Grigory with open satisfaction. In fact he was answering Fyodor Pavlovitch’s questions, and he knew it perfectly well, and he was deliberately pretending that Grigory had put them.
“Ivan,” Fyodor Pavlovitch cried suddenly, “lean down, let me whisper. He’s staged all this for your benefit. He wants you to praise him. Go on, praise him.”
Ivan listened to his father’s excited whisper with complete seriousness.
“Hold on, Smerdyakov, quiet for a minute,” cried Fyodor Pavlovitch again. “Ivan, give me your ear once more.”
Ivan bent down again, with a perfectly solemn face.
“I love you like I love Alyosha. Don’t think I don’t love you. Have some brandy?”
“Yes.—But you’re a bit drunk yourself,” thought Ivan, studying his father.
He was watching Smerdyakov with keen curiosity.
“You’re anathema accursed as it is,” Grigory suddenly burst out, “so how dare you argue, you scoundrel, after that, when—”
“Don’t scold him, Grigory, don’t scold him,” Fyodor Pavlovitch cut in.

“You ought to wait, Grigory Vassilyevitch, even for a short while, and listen, because I have not finished what I had to say. At the very moment I become accursed, at that same supreme moment, I am exactly like a heathen. My christening is taken from me and counts for nothing. Is that not so?”
“Get on and finish, my boy,” Fyodor Pavlovitch urged him, savoring a sip from his wine-glass.

“Now, if I have ceased to be a Christian, then I told the enemy no lie when they asked whether I was a Christian or not. God Himself had already relieved me of my Christianity, on account of the thought alone, before I had time to say a word to the enemy. And if I have already been discharged, then in what manner, and by what sort of justice, can I be held answerable as a Christian in the next world for denying Christ? Through the thought alone, before I denied Him, I had been relieved of my christening. If I am no longer a Christian, I cannot renounce Christ, for I have nothing left to renounce. Who will hold an unclean Tatar to account, Grigory Vassilyevitch, even in heaven, for not being born a Christian? And who would punish him for that, seeing that you can’t take two skins off one ox? Even if God Almighty did hold the Tatar to account, then when the Tatar dies, I imagine, God would give him the smallest punishment there is (since punished he must be). He would judge that the Tatar is not to blame for coming into the world an unclean heathen, the child of heathen parents. Surely the Lord God can’t take a Tatar and declare that he was a Christian? That would mean the Almighty was telling a real untruth. And can the Lord of Heaven and earth tell a lie, even in a single word?”

Grigory was thunderstruck. He stared at the orator, his eyes nearly popping out of his head. He did not clearly follow what had been said, but he had caught something in all this rigmarole, and he stood there like a man who has just banged his head against a wall. Fyodor Pavlovitch drained his glass and broke into his shrill laugh.

“Alyosha! Alyosha! What do you say to that! Ah, you casuist! He must have been with the Jesuits somewhere, Ivan. Oh, you stinking Jesuit, who taught you? But you’re talking nonsense, you casuist, nonsense, nonsense, nonsense. Don’t cry, Grigory, we’ll reduce him to smoke and ashes in a moment. Answer me this, you ass. Before your enemies you may be in the right, but in your own heart you renounced your faith all the same, and you say yourself that in that very hour you became anathema accursed. And once you’re anathema, they won’t give you a pat on the head for it in hell. What do you say to that, my fine Jesuit?”
“There is no doubt that I renounced it in my own heart, but there was no special sin in that. Or if there was a sin, it was a most ordinary one.”
“What do you mean, most ordinary?”
“You’re lying, you accursed man!” Grigory hissed.

“Think it over for yourself, Grigory Vassilyevitch,” Smerdyakov went on, sedate and unruffled. He was aware of his triumph, yet, as it were, generous toward the beaten foe. “Think it over for yourself, Grigory Vassilyevitch. The Scripture says that if you have faith as small as a mustard seed and tell a mountain to move into the sea, it will move at your word without the slightest delay. Very well, Grigory Vassilyevitch. I am without faith, and you have so great a faith that you swear at me constantly. So you try it. Tell this mountain to move, not into the sea, which is a long way off, but just into our stinking little river at the bottom of the garden. You will see for yourself that it will not budge. It will stay exactly where it is, however much you shout at it. That shows, Grigory Vassilyevitch, that you do not have faith in the proper manner, and only abuse other people about it. Consider this as well. In our day nobody, not only you but actually nobody, from the highest person to the lowest peasant, can push mountains into the sea—except perhaps one man in the whole world, or two at the most, and they are very likely saving their souls in secret somewhere in the Egyptian desert, so you would never find them. Now, if that is the case, and all the rest have no faith, will God curse all the rest? That is, the population of the entire earth, except for about two hermits in the desert? And in His well-known mercy, will He not forgive even one of them? And so I am convinced that although I may once have doubted, I shall be forgiven if I shed tears of repentance.”
“Wait!” cried Fyodor Pavlovitch, in a rapture of delight. “So you really suppose there are two who can move mountains? Ivan, make a note of it, write it down. That’s the Russian all over!”
“You are quite right that it is typical of the people’s faith,” Ivan agreed, with an approving smile.
“You agree! Then it must be so, if you agree. It’s true, isn’t it, Alyosha? That’s the Russian faith all over, isn’t it?”
“No, Smerdyakov doesn’t have the Russian faith at all,” said Alyosha, firmly and gravely.
“I’m not talking about his faith. I mean those two in the desert, only that notion. Surely that’s Russian?”
“Yes, that is purely Russian,” said Alyosha with a smile.

“Those words of yours are worth a gold piece, you ass, and I’ll hand it over to you today. But as for the rest, you talk nonsense, nonsense, nonsense. Let me tell you, you fool, that all of us here have little faith, but only through carelessness, because we haven’t the time. We’re overwhelmed with things to do. And second, the Lord God has given us so little time, only twenty-four hours in a day, that a man can’t even get enough sleep, let alone repent of his sins. Whereas you denied your faith to your enemies when you had nothing else on your mind but showing your faith! So I hold, brother, that it amounts to a sin.”

“It may amount to a sin, but kindly consider, Grigory Vassilyevitch, that if it does, it only makes the sin lighter. Suppose I had believed in very truth then, as I ought to have believed. Then it really would have been sinful if I had not endured torture for my faith and had gone over to the pagan Mohammedan religion. But of course it would not have come to torture, because I would only have had to say to the mountain at that moment, ‘Move and crush the tormentor,’ and it would have moved and crushed him that very instant like a black-beetle. I would have walked away as if nothing had happened, praising and glorifying God. But suppose I had tried all that at that very moment and cried to the mountain, ‘Crush these tormentors,’ and it had not crushed them. How could I have kept from doubting, I ask you, at such a time, in such a dreadful hour of mortal terror? And besides, I would know already that I could not reach the fullness of the Kingdom of Heaven (since the mountain had not moved at my word, they could not think much of my faith up above, and no very great reward could be waiting for me in the world to come). So why should I let them flay the skin off me as well, and to no good purpose? Even if they had skinned me half off my back, the mountain would still not have moved at my word or at my cry. And at such a moment not only might doubt come over a man, but he might lose his reason from fear and be unable to think at all. So how could I be especially to blame if, seeing no advantage or reward either there or here, I at least saved my skin? And so, trusting fully in the grace of the Lord, I would cherish the hope that I might be forgiven altogether.”
